item.title: EXCLUSIVE: Roc Nation CEO Desiree Perez Wins Sanctions After Daughter Destroyed Evidence
item.dc:creator: Grouchy Greg Watkins (@GrouchyGreg)
item.description: Desiree Perez secured an evidence-loss penalty against Demoree Hadley, while the judge kept her daughter's remaining claims alive.
item.content:encoded:
Desiree Perez won sanctions against her daughter, Demoree Hadley, after a federal judge found that Hadley deliberately destroyed evidence in their family legal battle.

U.S. District Judge Beth Bloom’s October 12 order gave the Roc Nation CEO an advantage if the dispute reaches a jury. Bloom refused to dismiss Hadley’s remaining claims, but ordered a jury instruction that presumes the missing evidence helped Perez and hurt her daughter.

The judge found that deleted messages and an alleged listening device were crucial to Perez’s defense against Hadley’s surveillance claims. Their destruction prevented Perez from investigating material her daughter had a duty to preserve.

Bloom explained her decision, referring to the lost texts, photos and videos as electronically stored information, or ESI: “Here, as Hadley testified, her deletion of text messages, photos, and videos, and destruction of the alleged listening device was not accidental or merely negligent. Rather, she voluntarily deleted the ESI and intentionally threw out the alleged listening device. Hadley should have known the listening device would need to be inspected and should have known to preserve the ESI. Instead, Hadley deleted the content from her phone and turned over only what she thought was relevant. Therefore, spoliation exists, warranting sanctions.”

The order cited Hadley’s testimony that she deleted more than 130,000 photos and videos but kept images of her grandparents. Hadley said she cleared her phone to free storage and wiped her iCloud account to prevent access she believed was illegal.

The mother-daughter dispute began when Hadley was detained in March 2024.

She sued in May 2025, claiming that Perez and others misused Florida’s Baker Act and Marchman Act to hold her in mental health facilities for nearly two weeks. Those laws cover involuntary mental health evaluation and substance abuse treatment.

Hadley accused her mother of using those proceedings to separate her from husband Javon Hadley.

Perez denied wrongdoing and said she acted to protect her daughter’s safety. She also sued Javon, alleging abuse that the couple denied.

item.title: MC Jin Joins Stephen Chow In “Kung Fu Soccer” English Version
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: MC Jin added his voice to Stephen Chow's latest film, which earned $344.4 million during China's summer box-office season.
item.content:encoded:
MC Jin joined the English voice cast of Stephen Chow’s “Kung Fu Soccer,” which will open in U.S. theaters October 23.

The new English version also featured voice performances from Chow and comedian Jimmy O. Yang. Distributor Encore Films announced that audiences in the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom and Ireland would get both the original-language film and the English dub.

Jin also joined the live-action ensemble alongside Yang. Zhang Xiaofei, Dilraba Dilmurat and Lay Zhang led the cast.

The film earned about $344.4 million during China’s June-through-August summer season, making it the country’s biggest movie of that period. The movie marked Chow’s first feature as a director since 2019’s “The New King of Comedy.”

The Western opening will arrive 25 years after “Shaolin Soccer,” the 2001 film in which Chow’s character Sing recruited his Shaolin brothers to form a soccer team.

“Stephen Chow’s films have always transcended language and cultural boundaries, bringing audiences together through his unique blend of action, comedy and heart,” Encore managing director Joyce Lee said.

“Kung Fu Soccer” put a women’s team at the center of that formula. The Emei Women’s Football Team rallied around captain Shuangshuang and striker Yulong, with mentor Xu Feng guiding the squad as it chased a championship. The players mixed soccer with martial arts as they competed in the Supreme Invincible Cup, facing doubts about their chances and setbacks that tested their teamwork.

The project also extended Jin’s connection with Chow. In December 2023, Jin released “Nobody” at the filmmaker’s invitation.

The song accompanied plans for Chow’s NFT collection of the same name, and its video drew on characters from his movies while featuring Chow’s voice. Their work together predated this film’s overseas release by nearly three years.

Jin’s seven-week winning run on BET’s “Freestyle Friday” led to his Ruff Ryders deal. He later recorded in both English and Chinese, building a career across those audiences.

Encore acquired distribution rights for the film outside mainland China in June. Cineplex listed the Mandarin version, with Chinese and English subtitles, for October 23. Encore also completed a Cantonese dub, with that version’s voice cast still to be announced.

The rapper also has a label with NE-YO, Pacific Music Group, which recently launched in Tokyo with the signing of Japanese rapper JP THE WAVY.

item.title: Busta Rhymes Picks A Tribe Called Quest’s “The Low End Theory” As Essential Listening
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Busta Rhymes chose A Tribe Called Quest's "The Low End Theory" for KCRW and revisited the studio memories behind his choice.
item.content:encoded:
Busta Rhymes chose A Tribe Called Quest’s The Low End Theory for KCRW’s “Must Listen,” returning to the classic album that he was featured on that helped boost his career.

The station released his episode Tuesday. The format sends guests through the station’s CD library to choose one essential album and leave a handwritten note for the next person who finds it.

KCRW’s episode announcement described a personal choice. Busta credited Q-Tip, Ali Shaheed Muhammad, Jarobi and the late Phife Dawg with recognizing his promise before he saw it himself.

He also recalled being at Battery Studios as the album took shape, while they still lived with their parents.

The connection went beyond fandom. Busta appeared with Leaders of the New School on “Scenario,” the closing track on the 1991 album. The appearance helped introduce him to a wider audience before his solo career.

The Low End Theory also marked a shift for Tribe after its 1990 debut. The 14-track album gave Phife Dawg a larger role alongside Q-Tip and brought jazz bassist Ron Carter onto “Verses From The Abstract.”

Songs such as “Rap Promoter” and “Show Business” addressed the problems young artists faced in the industry.

For Busta, the visit covered more than the record he ultimately chose. The episode announcement said he also pulled James Brown and Sly and the Family Stone from the shelves, pointing to their place in Hip-Hop’s musical roots and the drums that producers sampled.

His browsing also reached reggae and dancehall acts Shabba Ranks, Super Cat and The Skatalites, along with Fela Kuti.

The station visit grew out of his current work with another key figure in that musical history. Busta had come in the week before to speak with host Novena Carmel about Dillagence II, his project built around the late J Dilla’s beats.

Busta announced the project in August, continuing a recording partnership that dates back to his solo albums and the 2007 “Dillagence” mixtape.

The Library of Congress added The Low End Theory to the National Recording Registry in 2022. Busta’s “Must Listen” episode arrived in the year the album turned 35.

item.title: Drake Breaks The Temptations’ Record With 18th No. 1
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Drake passed Future and the Temptations with his 18th No. 1 R&B/Hip-Hop album after the "HABIBTI (FOMO)" expansion.
item.content:encoded:
Drake moved past Future and the Temptations for the most No. 1 albums on Billboard’s Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums chart, taking sole ownership of a record the Motown group had held or shared for 60 years.

HABIBTI became his 18th leader after climbing from No. 35 to No. 1 on the October 17 chart. Future and the Temptations each have 17, Billboard confirmed.

The album displaced another Drake release, ICEMAN. When the two arrived together in May, ICEMAN had kept HABIBTI out of the top spot.

It was the first self-replacement at No. 1 since Future and Metro Boomin traded places with their two joint albums in May 2024.

The latest climb followed the HABIBTI (FOMO) expansion, which brought four songs from Drake’s “FOMO” film to streaming services. “Solar Eclipse” paired him with Don Toliver over a reworking of Ella Langley’s “Choosin’ Texas,” while “Cold Shoulder” brought Toliver and Yebba together with Drake.

“Quebec” and “Classic PT2” completed the additions. The latter extended a song from the original album.

Drake had previewed the songs in his self-funded “FOMO” film, which premiered online in September. He told fans some of its music would reach streaming services, while warning that the film’s full soundtrack might not. The expanded version gave those four tracks an official home on HABIBTI, bringing the album to 15 songs.

That rollout followed an earlier surprise. Drake announced HABIBTI and MAID OF HONOUR during the fourth installment of his ICEMAN livestream, then released all three albums together on May 15. The trio marked his first solo album releases since 2023’s For All The Dogs.

For the tracking week ending October 8, HABIBTI earned 71,000 U.S. album-equivalent units, up 506%. Billboard combines the album’s editions when counting its chart total.

The project also rebounded to No. 2 on the all-genre Billboard 200, up from No. 116. Nearly 70,000 units came from streaming, driving its return to the top 10.

The Temptations first took the R&B album record with their third leader, “Gettin’ Ready,” in July 1966. They reached 17 with “A Song For You” in May 1975.

item.title: LUCKI Gives Long-Awaited Leaks An Official Release On “Last Laugh”
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: LUCKI scheduled "Last Laugh" for October 16, bringing decade-spanning archive tracks and fan-favorite leaks to streaming.
item.content:encoded:
LUCKI set an October 16 release for Last Laugh, an archive tape that will bring songs fans have chased through leaks and snippets onto streaming services.

The Chicago rapper announced the project Tuesday, drawing from recording sessions that span the past decade. “Overseas,” “60mgs” and “What It Is” are among the tracks slated for their first official release.

The collection will also include recordings that have never reached listeners, his team said in the announcement.

That mix gives longtime fans a chance to hear work that never made it onto his regular albums. Kodone created the cover art, which traces LUCKI’s different eras across 13 years. His career began as Lucki Eck$ with the 2013 tape “Alternative Trap.”

The move has a clear precedent in his catalog.

“Leave Her” circulated as a leak by at least 2021 before receiving a wide release in April 2023. Fans had pushed for the song after hearing it through unofficial SoundCloud uploads and TikTok clips. That wait ended with the BrentRambo-produced track landing on streaming platforms.

The archive tape follows “Dr*gs R Bad,” which entered the Billboard 200 at No. 9 in May with 51,000 equivalent album units. Its tracks earned 48.39 million on-demand official streams that week, his strongest streaming frame at the time.

Physical releases also played a role.

The album sold 6,000 copies in its opening week, his best sales week at the time, with several versions and signed editions helping that total. Last Laugh will be his second full-length release of 2026, turning attention from a new studio set to recordings from earlier sessions.

LUCKI’s own account of how he builds projects helps explain why a vault release can sound different from a single album.

In a 2019 interview, he said he chose songs and beats around a particular sound, rather than keeping every beat he liked.

“Even if I hear a good beat, if it doesn’t fit with the sound I want, I won’t pick it,” he told The FADER.

The announcement left more song titles to be revealed before Last Laugh arrives Friday.

item.title: YouTube Music Adds AI Song Labels With Rules For Beats & Vocals
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: YouTube Music began rolling out AI song labels while its rules separate generated vocals and lyrics from Auto-Tune and mastering.
item.content:encoded:
YouTube Music began labeling AI-generated songs on October 14 while drawing a line between machine-made music and familiar studio tools like Auto-Tune.

The labels focus on songs made mainly with generative AI.

The badge appears on the player page, and a tap opens more details about AI’s role. The company says the labels will also reach the main YouTube app. Labels draw on disclosures from music partners and YouTube’s detection tools.

For rappers, singers and beatmakers, the key is what counts as AI use. Google’s rules for music partners offer three choices: “Fully Gen AI,” “Partly Gen AI” and “No Gen AI.”

A prompt-built song with AI making the beat and voice falls into the first group. A generated bassline with live vocals and instruments fits the second. So does AI help with verses or a tune before the artist records it.

Using Auto-Tune to fix a sung note or an AI tool to master a track falls under “No Gen AI.” Google’s examples draw a line between those changes and using AI to make parts of the work itself.

The debate over AI in Hip-Hop began well before this rollout. AllHipHop reported in June 2025 that Swizz Beatz backed Timbaland’s move into AI during a livestream, while Young Guru warned about jobs for human singers, writers and producers.

The new rules also show why a badge needs context. Google lists a song with all-human audio but an AI-made music video as partly AI. That is a different use of the tool from having AI create the song itself, yet both involve AI.

Other groups draw the lines elsewhere.

On July 10, IFPI, the RIAA and a group of music organizations proposed voluntary “AI-Generated” and “AI-Assisted” labels for sound recordings. Their plan left out lyrics, composition, videos and cover art. Google’s examples, by contrast, include AI help with lyrics, tunes and videos.

“Fans want to know whether and how generative AI has been used in the music to which they listen,” IFPI and RIAA leaders said in their joint statement.

Tidal gives fans another choice: they can turn off tracks tagged as wholly AI-generated. Its support rules also say those recordings cannot earn royalties on Tidal. For now, it doesn’t apply to AI-made compositions alone.

item.title: AKA Trial Witness Describes Tibz Collapsing While Fleeing Gunfire
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: AKA's murder trial heard a witness describe running beside Tibz before he fell, as lawyers examined the shooting and aftermath.
item.content:encoded:
AKA‘s murder trial heard how a witness ran beside Tebello “Tibz” Motsoane as they fled gunfire, saw him fall and tried to get emergency help.

The witness told the Durban High Court on Wednesday, October 14, that he initially thought AKA had made it inside Wish restaurant. When he looked around and could not find the rapper, he went back outside and found him on the ground.

“He fell, and that is when I realized that he got shot,” the witness said of Motsoane, The Mercury reported.

The two victims had been embracing outside the restaurant when the shooting started. The witness said he was behind them, heard a loud noise and then several more shots before turning back toward the building with Motsoane alongside him.

He described repeated attempts to reach police and call an ambulance. He estimated it took about 10 minutes to reach police, who arrived about 15 minutes later. By the time officers reached the scene, he said, Motsoane had also died.

Defense lawyer Simphiwe Mlotshwa questioned the witness about whether any shots had been aimed at him. The exchange concerned an attempted-murder count in the case, which also covers the deaths of AKA and Motsoane.

“As you heard the shots, do you know or do you not know if there were any shots directed at you?” Mlotshwa asked, Eyewitness News reported.

The witness said he could not make sense of what was happening in the moment. He recalled sparks to his right and said the group ducked left into the restaurant.

Prosecutors also asked where AKA’s bodyguard had been. The witness said he last saw him before the shooting and could not say where he went afterward.

“I have no idea where he was; I did not see him anywhere,” he said, SABC News reported.

A second witness described Motsoane pushing himself against a wall to sit up despite his wounds, while people around the two men became distraught.

AKA, born Kiernan Forbes, and Motsoane were killed outside Wish on Durban’s Florida Road on February 10, 2023. Wednesday’s accounts followed earlier testimony about the shooting, but came from different witnesses.

Seven defendants pleaded not guilty when the trial opened on October 5. They face charges including conspiracy to commit murder, two murders, attempted murder and firearm offenses. The trial continued Wednesday.

item.title: Muni Long Wins Fight To Keep Medical Records From Ex-Managers
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Muni Long won a medical privacy fight with her former managers as their lawsuit over unpaid fees and a clinic stay continued.
item.content:encoded:
Muni Long won a fight to keep her medical records private after her former managers tried to obtain files from her 2024 stay at a mental health facility.

U.S. Magistrate Judge Sarah Netburn recently blocked the request. She also barred Ebony Son Entertainment, the company run by Chaka Zulu and Jeff Dixon, from getting the same treatment details by questioning Long herself.

The records fight grew out of a serious accusation from the singer’s team.

Her representatives claimed the managers took her phone and tried to have her committed against her will while she was suffering from a lupus flare-up. Ebony Son denied that account and sued over what it said was a false statement that damaged its reputation.

The company wanted records from Cleveland Clinic Indian River Behavioral Health Center covering Long’s March 2024 admission, diagnosis and treatment. It argued those files offered the best evidence of what happened.

Long, whose legal name is Priscilla Renea Hamilton, had brought her own claim that the managers intentionally caused her emotional distress. But she dropped that claim before releasing any records, restoring her right to keep them private.

Netburn wrote in the five-page order:

“Hamilton’s initial counterclaim for intentional infliction of emotional distress put her mental health at issue and, thus, would have waived her privilege. But Hamilton never released her records before she withdrew the counterclaim, and therefore her privilege was reinstated.”

The case began as a fight over management fees. Ebony Son’s original federal lawsuit sought more than $612,000, including $458,600 in commissions and more than $153,000 in expenses.

The company claimed Long agreed to pay 20% of the gross revenue from work it helped secure or support. It accused her of stopping payments after October 2024, even as she continued earning money from those deals.

Long’s team disputed the debt and said no formal contract existed.

In an early court response, she described a trial management arrangement and discussions about paying 20% of net revenue only from opportunities the managers brought her.

Netburn rejected Ebony Son’s argument that its own lawsuit entitled it to Long’s medical files.

But it left room to question how Long entered the clinic, as long as they did not reveal protected medical information. Netburn wrote:

“Plaintiff may, however, seek non-medical information from Hamilton regarding the alleged defamatory statement and the circumstances surrounding her admission to the Clinic, to the extent it would not pierce her privilege. Thus, Defendants’ motion for a protective order is granted insofar as it seeks information protected by the patient-doctor/psychotherapist privilege, but denied insofar as it seeks non-treatment related information from Hamilton regarding her admission.”

Netburn ordered Ebony Son to send the ruling to the clinic and tell it to disregard the demand for Long’s records.

item.title: Marsha Blackburn Roasted For Kendrick Lamar AI Slop Campaign Clip
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Marsha Blackburn's AI take on Kendrick Lamar's Super Bowl set drew a rebuke from her rival and revived her past clash with rap.
item.content:encoded:
Marsha Blackburn drew backlash after her campaign used an AI-generated remake of Kendrick Lamar’s Super Bowl performance to promote early voting in Tennessee’s governor’s race.

The Republican senator posted the clip on X Tuesday with the caption, “Tomorrow. Ready to roll.” The post quickly became a target for critics, including her Democratic opponent, Jerri Green.

The clip cast Blackburn in the role of Kendrick Lamar and used his Drake diss “Not Like Us,” Mediaite reported. It also depicted Rep. Tim Burchett, Sen. Bill Hagerty, Tennessee state Sen. Brent Taylor and Knox County Mayor Glenn Jacobs as dancers. Jacobs appeared as Kane, the masked character he played in WWE.

Green shared the campaign’s post and took aim at its use of artificial intelligence.

“When I say please stop using AI to support our campaign, this is what I mean…” Green wrote.

The criticism also revived Blackburn’s earlier clash with rap artists. In 2007, she took part in a House hearing on stereotypes and degrading images in entertainment. Master P and David Banner testified as lawmakers questioned the messages in Hip-Hop lyrics.

“How and when did society fail you that you would choose to write such filth?” Blackburn asked, as POLITICO documented at the time.

Kendrick Lamar’s song moved far beyond its origins in his 2024 battle with Drake. “Not Like Us” won five Grammy Awards in 2025 before he performed it during his Super Bowl halftime show. That set also featured SZA, Samuel L. Jackson, Mustard and Serena Williams.

Blackburn has since become a sponsor of legislation aimed at protecting artists from AI copies of their voices and faces. Her office announced in June that the bipartisan NO FAKES Act advanced out of the Senate Judiciary Committee. The proposal’s stated focus was digital replicas made without a person’s consent.

“AI should empower innovation, not give scammers and online predators a free pass to exploit someone’s voice and visual likeness without permission,” Blackburn said in that announcement.

She said those safeguards should cover artists, songwriters, students and other Americans. Blackburn described the bill as a way to shield Tennessee’s creative community and creators across the country from digital impersonation. She called the committee vote a step toward making those rules law.

item.title: G Herbo Fraud Co-Defendant Avoids Prison After Hung Jury
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: G Herbo co-defendant Steven Hayes Jr. avoided prison after a hung jury and guilty plea in the stolen-card luxury spending case.
item.content:encoded:
G Herbo’s fraud co-defendant Steven Hayes Jr. avoided prison for his part in the stolen-card scheme that paid for jets, villas and designer puppies.

U.S. District Judge Mark G. Mastroianni sentenced Hayes, 34, to three years’ probation on October 8 in Springfield, Massachusetts. Prosecutors had sought four to six months in prison. The Justice Department announced the sentence October 14.

Hayes was held responsible for $44,814 in victim losses. The judge ordered him to pay $2,728 in restitution and forfeit the same amount.

The case went to trial in February, but jurors could not agree on a verdict. Hayes then pleaded guilty in May to conspiracy to commit wire fraud. Prosecutors charged six men in the case in 2020.

“Hayes and his co-conspirators used illicit account information to obtain, among other things, a private jet charter flight, a New York City villa rental, designer puppies from a pet boutique and car insurance. In total, Hayes was responsible for $44,814 in victim losses,” the Justice Department stated.

The purchases went through because the stolen card details belonged to real people. Once the card owners spotted charges they had not made, they disputed them. Card companies reversed the payments, leaving the businesses that supplied flights, lodging and goods with the losses.

G Herbo, whose legal name is Herbert Wright III, received his own probation sentence on January 11, 2024. He had pleaded guilty the previous July to wire fraud conspiracy and lying to a federal official.

His plea deal also led prosecutors to drop charges of aggravated identity theft.

The judge ordered the rapper to pay $139,968 in restitution and forfeiture, plus a $5,500 fine. His lawyers asked the judge to weigh his remorse, growth as a father and community work. They argued that he should stay out of prison.

Prosecutors said G Herbo used the fraud proceeds to travel to shows and post photos that promoted his career.

Those pictures showed him on private jets, in luxury cars and at a Jamaican villa. He also lied to a federal agent in November 2018, denying that he worked with or received help from promoter Antonio Strong.

Strong pleaded guilty in May 2024 and received nearly three years in prison that October. His scheme went beyond trips: prosecutors said he used fake names and claimed ties to music companies such as Sony and Universal to make fraudulent purchases.

Three other defendants, Joseph Williams, Demario Sorrells and celebrity barber Terrence Bender, also received probation.

Hayes’ sentence followed the earlier guilty pleas and punishments of all five of his co-defendants.
